assessment.nuance: Penicillin cures syphilis at every stage, though damage from late syphilis is permanent; congenital syphilis is preventable by testing in pregnancy.

assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D002690)

assessment.nuance: Antibiotics cure gonorrhoea, but resistance is rising and few effective drugs remain.
Metronidazole cures it.
Lifelong infection; antivirals shorten outbreaks and suppressive treatment prevents most recurrences.

sources.title: Herpes simplex virus fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of other sexually transmitted infections; most bacterial and parasitic ones are curable with antimicrobials.

sources.title: Sexually transmitted infections fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: A 4-6 month course of standard drugs cures about 85% of patients; most deaths are in people never diagnosed or treated.
Most pneumonia is cured by antibiotics (bacterial) or resolves with supportive care (viral); it is still the leading infectious killer of young children where oxygen and antibiotics are out of reach.

sources.title: Pneumonia in children fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Colds and sore throats resolve on their own within days; antibiotics cure strep throat.
Most ear infections clear on their own or with antibiotics; chronic suppurative otitis media can cause hearing loss.
Most people recover fully; antivirals and steroids reduce severe disease and death in high-risk patients. Some develop long COVID.
Oral rehydration solution and zinc cure most diarrhoea; deaths come from dehydration where these simple treatments do not reach.
Antibiotics cure typhoid, but extensively drug-resistant strains are spreading in South Asia. Vaccines prevent it.
Antibiotics cure paratyphoid, as for typhoid; drug resistance is a growing problem.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D010284)

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of other intestinal infections; most resolve with rehydration or antimicrobials.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D007411, D005759)

assessment.nuance: Artemisinin-based combination therapy cures uncomplicated malaria; severe malaria needs injectable artesunate. Partial artemisinin resistance is spreading in Africa.
Benznidazole or nifurtimox cures the infection when given early, but most patients are diagnosed in the chronic phase, when heart and gut damage can only be managed.
Kala-azar is fatal untreated, but liposomal amphotericin B or other drugs cure over 90% of patients.
Skin sores often heal on their own within months, leaving scars; antimony drugs and other treatments speed healing. Mucosal forms are harder to treat.
Fatal untreated, but oral fexinidazole (and acoziborole) now cure it; cases have fallen below 1,000 a year.

sources.title: Trypanosomiasis, human African (sleeping sickness) fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Praziquantel cures the infection and mass treatment controls it; reinfection is common and long-term organ damage may persist.
Neurocysticercosis is treated with antiparasitic drugs, steroids and antiseizure medicines, which control seizures in most patients; some need surgery.
Surgery, drainage (PAIR) or albendazole cures most hydatid cysts; some recur.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D004443)

assessment.nuance: Mass drug administration clears the parasite and has eliminated it in many countries, but lymphoedema and elephantiasis are lifelong and managed with hygiene and care; hydrocele is cured by surgery.

Yearly or twice-yearly ivermectin kills the microfilariae and stops progression, and has eliminated transmission in some countries; it does not kill adult worms, and blindness already caused is permanent.
Azithromycin cures the infection and surgery corrects in-turned eyelashes; blindness already caused is permanent. Trachoma has been eliminated in over 20 countries.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D014141)

assessment.nuance: No antiviral treats it; supportive care helps, but up to half of severe cases die. A single vaccine dose gives lifelong protection.
Almost always fatal once symptoms appear; prompt post-exposure vaccination after a bite prevents it completely.
A single dose of albendazole or mebendazole cures it; reinfection is common without sanitation.

sources.title: Soil-transmitted helminth infections fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Albendazole or mebendazole treats it, though cure rates are lower than for other worms; reinfection is common.

sources.title: Soil-transmitted helminth infections fact sheet, WHO

assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D014257)

assessment.nuance: Albendazole or mebendazole cures it, and iron corrects the anaemia it causes; reinfection is common without sanitation.

sources.title: Soil-transmitted helminth infections fact sheet, WHO

assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D006725)

assessment.nuance: Praziquantel or triclabendazole cures liver, lung and intestinal fluke infections.

sources.title: Foodborne trematode infections fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Multidrug therapy, free through WHO, cures leprosy; nerve damage and disability already present are permanent.
Monoclonal antibodies (for Zaire ebolavirus) and early supportive care have cut mortality, but outbreaks still kill around a third or more of patients; a vaccine prevents it.
No specific treatment; most infections are mild and resolve, but infection in pregnancy can cause microcephaly and other lifelong birth defects.
No drug or vaccine exists, but the worm is removed by slowly winding it out; the disease is close to eradication, with only a handful of human cases a year.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D004320)

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of other neglected tropical diseases; most are curable with antiparasitic or antibiotic drugs, though some chronic damage is permanent.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D058069, D014330)

assessment.nuance: Bacterial meningitis is curable with prompt antibiotics, but about one in six patients dies and one in five survivors has lasting effects; viral meningitis usually resolves on its own.
Aciclovir treats herpes encephalitis, but most viral encephalitis has no specific treatment; many survivors have lasting brain damage.
Diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics cure most patients, though up to 10% die and antitoxin is in short supply. Vaccination prevents it.
Antibiotics clear the infection, especially early; the cough lasts weeks, and infants can die. Vaccination prevents it.
Antitoxin, wound care, muscle relaxants and intensive care save many, but tetanus is often fatal where ventilation is unavailable. Vaccination prevents it.
No antiviral treats measles; supportive care and vitamin A reduce deaths, and most children recover, but it kills and disables where care is poor. Vaccination prevents it.
Chickenpox resolves on its own and antivirals help high-risk patients; shingles resolves too, but post-herpetic nerve pain can last.
Self-limiting: almost everyone recovers fully with supportive care; vaccination prevents it.
Most adults clear acute hepatitis B on their own with supportive care; infants usually do not, and develop chronic infection. Vaccination prevents it.
Direct-acting antivirals cure over 95% of hepatitis C infections in 8-12 weeks; most infections are undiagnosed.
Usually self-limiting with full recovery; it is dangerous in pregnancy, and can become chronic in immunosuppressed people.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D016751)

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of other infectious diseases; most are curable with antimicrobials, outcomes vary.
Uterotonic drugs, tranexamic acid, transfusion and surgery stop most postpartum bleeding; it is still the leading cause of maternal death where emergency care is lacking.

368.name: Maternal sepsis and other maternal infections

assessment.nuance: Antibiotics cure most maternal infections when given promptly; sepsis is still a leading cause of maternal death where care is delayed.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D011645, D011251)

assessment.nuance: Delivery ends pre-eclampsia; blood-pressure drugs and magnesium sulfate prevent seizures and death until then.

370.name: Maternal obstructed labor and uterine rupture

assessment.nuance: Caesarean section resolves obstructed labour; where it is unavailable, it causes uterine rupture, fistula and death.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D004420, D014597, D007744)

assessment.nuance: Complications of miscarriage and abortion are treated with medicines or minor procedures; unsafe abortion still causes many maternal deaths.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D000022)

assessment.nuance: Methotrexate or surgery treats it; a ruptured ectopic pregnancy is an emergency and can be fatal without surgery.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D011271)

assessment.nuance: Deaths from pre-existing conditions made worse by pregnancy; outcomes depend on the underlying disease.
Deaths from obstetric causes more than six weeks after the end of pregnancy; outcomes depend on the underlying condition.
Antiretroviral therapy in pregnancy controls HIV and prevents transmission to the baby.

sources.title: HIV and AIDS fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of other direct obstetric complications; most resolve with obstetric care.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D011248, D007744)

assessment.nuance: Neonatal care (warmth, kangaroo care, steroids before birth, breathing support) saves most preterm babies where it exists, but complications cause lasting disability in some, and survival is far lower in low-income countries.

382.name: Neonatal encephalopathy due to birth asphyxia and trauma

assessment.nuance: Therapeutic cooling reduces death and disability in babies with moderate or severe encephalopathy, but brain injury already done is permanent; many survivors have cerebral palsy.

sources.title: Newborn mortality fact sheet, WHO (birth asphyxia and trauma)

383.name: Neonatal sepsis and other neonatal infections

assessment.nuance: Prompt antibiotics cure most newborn infections, but mortality is high where diagnosis is late, and antibiotic resistance is rising.

384.name: Hemolytic disease and other neonatal jaundice

assessment.nuance: Phototherapy, and exchange transfusion in severe cases, clear newborn jaundice; untreated severe jaundice causes permanent brain damage (kernicterus).
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D007567, D004899)

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of newborn conditions; outcomes vary widely and depend on access to neonatal care.
Ready-to-use therapeutic food cures most children with severe acute malnutrition, but few who need it receive it; stunting from chronic undernutrition is largely irreversible.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D011502, D000067011)

assessment.nuance: Vitamin A supplements correct the deficiency; blindness from corneal damage is permanent.

sources.title: Vitamin A deficiency, WHO Nutrition Landscape Information System

assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D014802, D014985)

assessment.nuance: Iron supplements and diet correct iron-deficiency anaemia; it recurs if the cause (poor diet, blood loss, worms) persists.
A residual GBD group of nutritional deficiencies (e.g. iodine, vitamins); supplementation corrects most of them.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D003677, D018977)

assessment.nuance: Curable by surgery and radiotherapy when small; many patients, especially in South Asia, present late. 5-year survival about 69% (oral cavity and pharynx).

sources.title: Lip and Oral Cavity Cancer Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Oral Cavity and Pharynx Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Chemoradiotherapy cures many patients with early or locoregional disease (it is highly radiosensitive), but overall 5-year survival is roughly 60-70%, below the bar used for Curable cancers; distant metastases are treatable, not curable. Changed from Curable after the blind second opinion (SECOND-OPINION.md).
Oropharynx and hypopharynx cancers. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer is cured in most patients; HPV-negative and hypopharyngeal cancers do much worse.
Usually diagnosed late; chemoradiotherapy and surgery cure a minority. 5-year survival about 22%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Esophageal Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Gastrectomy cures early gastric cancer, but most cases are found late; 5-year survival is about 36%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Stomach Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Curable when caught early (surgery for localized disease, 5-year survival about 90%); about 65% survive 5 years overall, and metastatic disease is treated, not cured.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Colorectal Cancer, SEER

417.name: Liver cancer
members: Liver cancer due to hepatitis B
Liver cancer due to hepatitis C
Liver cancer due to alcohol use
Liver cancer due to other causes

assessment.nuance: Resection, ablation or transplant can cure early liver cancer, but most patients present with advanced disease; systemic therapy extends survival. 5-year survival about 22%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Liver and Intrahepatic Bile Duct Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Chemotherapy plus complete resection or liver transplant cures about 80% of children.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D018197)

assessment.nuance: Usually found late; surgery cures only early cases (often found incidentally at gallbladder removal).
Only about one in five patients can have surgery; chemotherapy extends life modestly. 5-year survival about 13%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Pancreatic Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Early laryngeal cancer is often cured by radiotherapy or surgery with the voice preserved; advanced cases need laryngectomy. 5-year survival about 62%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Laryngeal Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Curable by surgery or radiotherapy when found at stage I, but most patients are diagnosed with advanced disease; targeted and immune therapies extend survival. SEER 5-year relative survival about 27%.

sources.title: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Lung and Bronchus Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Most melanomas are found thin and localized and are cured by excision (SEER 5-year survival about 94%). Immunotherapy now gives durable control in a share of metastatic cases.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Melanoma of the Skin, SEER

assessment.nuance: Cutaneous squamous-cell carcinoma is cured by excision or other local treatment in the vast majority of cases; a small share spreads, mainly in immunosuppressed patients.

1011.name: Soft tissue and other extraosseous sarcomas

assessment.nuance: Wide surgical excision with radiotherapy cures many localized sarcomas; metastatic disease is rarely curable. 5-year survival about 66%.

sources.title: Adult Soft Tissue Sarcoma Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Soft Tissue including Heart Cancer, SEER

1012.name: Malignant neoplasm of bone and articular cartilage

assessment.nuance: Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma are cured in about two-thirds of patients with localized disease; metastatic disease has a poor outlook. 5-year survival about 69%.

sources.title: Osteosarcoma and Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma of Bone Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Bone and Joint Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Most patients are diagnosed with localized or regional disease and are cured by surgery with radiotherapy and systemic therapy (SEER 5-year survival about 91%). Metastatic breast cancer is treatable, not curable; outcomes are much worse where screening and treatment are scarce.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Female Breast Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Curable when found early through screening (surgery or chemoradiation); globally most deaths are in women diagnosed late. SEER 5-year survival about 67%. Largely preventable by HPV vaccination and screening.
Most endometrial cancers are found at stage I because of early bleeding and are cured by hysterectomy. SEER 5-year survival about 81%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Uterine Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Most cases are found at an advanced stage; surgery and platinum chemotherapy (plus PARP inhibitors) give long remissions, but most relapse. 5-year survival about 52%.

sources.title: Ovarian Epithelial, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancer Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Ovarian Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Most cases are found localized and are cured by surgery or radiotherapy, or need no treatment at all (active surveillance). SEER 5-year survival about 98%. Metastatic disease is controlled for years by hormone therapy but not cured.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Prostate Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Cured in more than 95% of patients with orchiectomy and, when needed, platinum chemotherapy, even when it has spread.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Testicular Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Localized tumours (most cases) are often cured by nephrectomy; advanced disease is treated with immunotherapy and targeted drugs. 5-year survival about 78%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Kidney and Renal Pelvis Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Most cases are non-muscle-invasive and removed endoscopically, but they recur often and need lifelong surveillance; invasive disease needs cystectomy or chemoradiation. 5-year survival about 78%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Bladder Cancer, SEER

477.name: Brain and central nervous system cancer

assessment.nuance: Covers many tumour types. The commonest malignant one in adults, glioblastoma, is treated with surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide but rarely cured; some low-grade and childhood tumours are curable.

sources.title: Adult Central Nervous System Tumors Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Brain and Other Nervous System Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Cured in over 95% of children in high-income countries, usually with sight preserved; survival is far lower in low-income countries because of late diagnosis.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D012175)

assessment.nuance: Mostly uveal melanoma in adults: radiotherapy or enucleation controls the eye tumour, but about half of patients later develop liver metastases.

1013.name: Neuroblastoma and other peripheral nervous cell tumors

assessment.nuance: Low- and intermediate-risk neuroblastoma is usually cured, but about half of patients have high-risk disease, with about 50% long-term survival despite intensive therapy.
Mostly differentiated thyroid cancer, cured by surgery with or without radioiodine; SEER 5-year survival about 98%. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is rare and rarely curable.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Thyroid Cancer, SEER

assessment.nuance: Rarely curable; chemotherapy and immunotherapy extend survival, which is usually 1-2 years from diagnosis.
Cured in most patients with chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy; SEER 5-year survival about 89%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Hodgkin Lymphoma, SEER

assessment.nuance: Intensive chemotherapy cures about 90% of children and most adults in high-income settings; survival is much lower in sub-Saharan Africa, where most cases occur.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D002051)

assessment.nuance: A mixed group. The commonest aggressive type (diffuse large B-cell) is cured in about 60-70% of patients; indolent types such as follicular lymphoma are controlled for years but relapse. SEER 5-year survival about 74%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma, SEER

assessment.nuance: Not curable; modern combinations (proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, anti-CD38 antibodies, CAR-T) give years of remission. 5-year survival about 62%.

sources.title: Plasma Cell Neoplasms (Including Multiple Myeloma) Treatment (PDQ), NCI

assessment.nuance: Curable in about 90% of children, the majority of patients; adults fare worse (around 40% long-term survival).

sources.title: Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia, SEER

assessment.nuance: Often needs no treatment for years; when it does, BTK and BCL-2 inhibitors keep most patients in long remission. Not curable, but many live a near-normal lifespan. SEER 5-year survival about 89%.

sources.title: Cancer Stat Facts: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia, SEER

assessment.nuance: Intensive chemotherapy and stem-cell transplant cure some younger patients, but most patients are older; 5-year survival about 33%.

sources.title: Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treatment (PDQ), NCI
Cancer Stat Facts: Acute Myeloid Leukemia, SEER

assessment.nuance: Tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (imatinib and successors) give most patients a near-normal life expectancy on daily treatment; some can stop treatment after deep remission.
A residual GBD group of leukaemias not listed separately; outcomes vary by type.
A residual GBD group of cancers not listed elsewhere; outcomes vary widely by site.

964.name: Myelodysplastic, myeloproliferative, and other hematopoietic neoplasms

assessment.nuance: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia) are often controlled for decades; myelodysplastic syndromes are mostly treatable but not curable without a stem-cell transplant.

965.name: Benign and in situ intestinal neoplasms

assessment.nuance: Colorectal polyps and in situ tumours are cured by removal at colonoscopy; that is the point of screening.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D003111, D007417)

966.name: Benign and in situ cervical and uterine neoplasms

assessment.nuance: Cervical precancer (CIN) is cured by excision or ablation, which is why screening prevents cervical cancer.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D002578, D065310)

1164.name: Other benign and in situ neoplasms

assessment.nuance: Benign and in situ tumours are usually cured by removal when they need treatment at all.
Penicillin prophylaxis stops progression and valve surgery can restore function, but established valve damage is permanent and most patients live where surgery is out of reach.

sources.title: Rheumatic heart disease fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Statins, antiplatelets, blood-pressure control and stenting or bypass let most patients live near-normal lives, but it remains the world's leading cause of death, much of it where care is not reached in time.

Clot-busting drugs and thrombectomy can reverse a stroke if given within hours, but most patients worldwide do not reach them in time; rehabilitation and secondary prevention limit disability and recurrence.

No treatment reverses the bleed itself; acute blood-pressure control, reversal of anticoagulants, sometimes surgery, and rehabilitation limit harm. About 40% die within a month and many survivors are left disabled.
Aneurysm coiling or clipping prevents re-bleeding, but about a third of patients die and many survivors have lasting deficits.
Controlling blood pressure with cheap, effective drugs prevents and partly reverses hypertensive heart damage; once heart failure develops it is treatable, not curable.
No drug slows it, but surgical or transcatheter valve replacement restores near-normal life expectancy once symptoms appear.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Controlled but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D001024)

assessment.nuance: Surgical repair of a degenerative (prolapsing) mitral valve is durable and restores normal life expectancy when done in time; transcatheter repair serves patients too frail for surgery.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D008944, D008945)

assessment.nuance: Mainly tricuspid and pulmonary valve disease: watched, treated with diuretics, and repaired or replaced when needed.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Controlled but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D006349, D014262)

assessment.nuance: Most viral myocarditis resolves with supportive and heart-failure treatment; a minority progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy or needs a transplant.
Heart-failure drugs and devices improve survival substantially, but most cardiomyopathies progress; heart transplant is the only cure.
Anticoagulation prevents most strokes and rate or rhythm control relieves symptoms; catheter ablation cures some patients. Most live near-normal lives on treatment.
Planned open or endovascular repair of a large aneurysm removes the risk of rupture; small aneurysms are watched. Rupture is fatal in most cases, which is why screening matters.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D001014, D017544)

assessment.nuance: Exercise, smoking cessation, statins, antiplatelets and revascularisation relieve symptoms and lower cardiovascular risk; the disease itself is not reversed.
Weeks of intravenous antibiotics, with valve surgery in about half of cases, cure most patients, but in-hospital mortality is still around 15-20%.
A residual GBD group (e.g. venous and lymphatic disorders, conduction disorders, pericardial disease); outcomes vary.
Lung damage is irreversible; stopping smoking slows decline, and inhalers, pulmonary rehabilitation and oxygen ease symptoms and cut flare-ups.

sources.title: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Lung scarring from silica dust is permanent and can progress after exposure stops; care is supportive (oxygen, rehabilitation), with lung transplant for a few.

sources.title: About Silica and Worker Health, NIOSH/CDC

assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Untreatable but ChEMBL has 1 approved drug for D012829

assessment.nuance: Asbestos-caused lung fibrosis is permanent and often progressive; treatment is supportive.
Black lung is irreversible and progressive massive fibrosis can worsen after exposure ends; care is supportive.
Other dust-caused lung fibrosis; no therapy reverses or halts it, so care is supportive and prevention is the only real tool.

sources.title: COPD fact sheet, WHO (occupational dust exposure)

assessment.nuance: Inhaled corticosteroids and relievers let most people live normal lives; poor access to inhalers drives most asthma deaths.

sources.title: Asthma: Treatment and Action Plan, NHLBI

516.name: Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary sarcoidosis

assessment.nuance: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is slowed by antifibrotic drugs but not stopped; sarcoidosis often resolves on its own or with steroids.
A residual GBD group of chronic respiratory diseases; most are managed rather than cured.

521.name: Cirrhosis and other chronic liver diseases

assessment.nuance: Treating the cause (hepatitis C is curable, hepatitis B suppressible, alcohol stopped) can halt and partly reverse fibrosis; established cirrhosis is managed, and transplant is the only cure for end-stage disease.

971.name: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease including cirrhosis

assessment.nuance: Weight loss can reverse fatty liver; resmetirom and semaglutide are now approved for MASH with fibrosis, but there is no cure for advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis other than transplant.

sources.title: Treatment for Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease, NIDDK

assessment.nuance: Eradicating H. pylori and stopping NSAIDs, with acid-suppressing drugs, heals most ulcers and prevents recurrence.

sources.title: Peptic Ulcers (Stomach and Duodenal Ulcers), NIDDK

assessment.nuance: Treating the cause (H. pylori eradication, stopping NSAIDs or alcohol) with acid suppression heals most gastritis and duodenitis.

sources.title: Treatment for Gastritis and Gastropathy, NIDDK

assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D005756, D004382)

assessment.nuance: Proton-pump inhibitors and lifestyle changes control symptoms and heal oesophagitis in most patients; anti-reflux surgery is an option for some.

sources.title: Treatment for GER and GERD, NIDDK

assessment.nuance: Appendicectomy (or antibiotics for uncomplicated cases) cures it; delayed treatment risks perforation.
Most bowel obstructions resolve with bowel rest or are relieved by surgery; outcomes depend on the cause and on prompt access to surgery.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D007415, D007418)

assessment.nuance: Surgical repair, open or laparoscopic, cures the hernia; recurrence is uncommon.
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D006552, D006550, D046449)

assessment.nuance: Aminosalicylates, steroids, immunosuppressants and biologics keep most patients in remission; colectomy removes the disease when drugs fail.
Not curable, but immunosuppressants and biologics keep most patients in remission and leading normal lives; many still need surgery at some point.
Acute mesenteric ischaemia needs emergency revascularisation or bowel resection and is often fatal; chronic forms can be relieved by stenting.
Mostly gallstone disease: symptomatic gallstones are cured by removing the gallbladder (laparoscopic cholecystectomy).
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Curable but ChEMBL has no approved drug (D042882, D002764, D002769)

assessment.nuance: Most acute pancreatitis is mild and resolves with supportive hospital care and treatment of the cause (gallstones, alcohol); severe attacks can be fatal, and chronic pancreatitis is managed, not cured.
A residual GBD group of digestive diseases (e.g. diverticular and functional bowel disorders); outcomes vary.
Cholinesterase inhibitors ease symptoms, and the anti-amyloid antibodies lecanemab and donanemab modestly slow early Alzheimer's; nothing stops or reverses dementia.
Levodopa and other drugs, plus deep-brain stimulation, control symptoms for years; nothing slows the underlying neurodegeneration.
About 70% of people become seizure-free on antiseizure medicines; surgery helps some of the rest. Three-quarters of people in low-income countries go untreated.
Disease-modifying therapies, especially high-efficacy ones started early, greatly reduce relapses and slow disability; progressive forms respond poorly and there is no cure.
No treatment stops ALS. Riluzole and edaravone slow progression modestly, and tofersen helps the rare SOD1 form; care is supportive (breathing and feeding support).
assessment.crossCheck: flag: claims Untreatable but ChEMBL has 3 approved drugs for D000690

assessment.nuance: Acute treatments (triptans, gepants) and preventives (including CGRP antibodies) cut the number and severity of attacks; there is no cure.

sources.title: Migraine and other headache disorders fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: Episodes respond to simple painkillers; chronic tension-type headache can be eased by amitriptyline and avoiding medication overuse.

sources.title: Migraine and other headache disorders fact sheet, WHO

assessment.nuance: A residual GBD group of neurological disorders (e.g. neuropathies, other neurodegenerative diseases); mostly managed rather than cured.
